findings.summary: The gap's claim that 'No study has measured spindle trains in older adults' is false. Champetier et al. (SLEEP 2022/23) measured age-related changes in fast-spindle temporal clustering (0.02-Hz infraslow periodicity) in 147 older vs 32 young-to-middle-aged adults and related clustering to sleep-dependent memory consolidation in 57 older adults. A 2025 SLEEP study tested spindles clustered in trains as a modulator of overnight episodic memory consolidation in 42 healthy older adults, and a 2025 Sleep Advances paper characterised spindle clusters in younger vs older adults. Already answered: whether spindle clustering/trains decline with age, and whether they relate to (declarative/episodic) consolidation in older adults. Still open: whether loss of trains, rather than isolated-spindle density, mediates the age-related deficit in overnight motor-sequence consolidation, for example via reanalysis of the n=173 gross-motor PSG dataset.

The gap says 'no claim reports CLAS tested on a procedural/motor outcome in healthy older adults', but this has been done. Schneider et al. (SLEEP 2020) applied one night of auditory closed-loop SO-up-state stimulation to 17 healthy middle-aged/older adults (55.7 ± 1.0 y). Outcomes included overnight finger-tapping procedural consolidation: stimulation had no effect (t(16) = -1.01, p = .33), and SO/spindle responses were weaker than in young adults. Multi-night (3-night) PLAS has also been run in healthy older adults (mean age 68.9). It increased SO-coupled spindles by 24%, but only declarative/verbal outcomes were tested. CLAS effects on SO, spindles, coupling and motor procedural consolidation have been studied in young adults (Sleep 2023). Already answered: single-night CLAS → finger-tapping in ~56-year-olds (null), and multi-night CLAS boosting coupling in healthy older adults. Still open: multi-night CLAS with a motor-sequence outcome in adults aged 60+, and formal mediation by SO–spindle coupling.

The premise that open-loop nap TMR in older adults is uniformly null is mis-stated. Johnson et al. (Neurosci Lett 2020) found that TMR during a 1-h nap improved sensorimotor (non-dominant-arm throwing) accuracy in healthy older adults; the gap omits this positive result. Overnight TMR in older adults is also not untested: Cordi et al. (2018) applied overnight NREM TMR to adults over 60 (vocabulary; no benefit). Closed-loop SO-up-state TMR for motor sequences works in young adults (Nat Commun 2025). Multi-night sleep-cued TMR for motor (gait) rehabilitation is registered in older stroke and PD patients (StimuLOOP trials). Still open: phase-targeted (SO up-state) overnight TMR of a motor sequence in healthy older adults. The gap should cite the mixed (not null) older-adult TMR evidence.

Training closely followed by sleep has already been compared with training far from sleep in older adults. In elderly participants, evening (6–9 pm) vs morning multi-session motor training gave better long-term retention (Front Aging Neurosci 2019). Evening finger-tapping practice in the elderly produced additional overnight and 1-week gains plus offline reorganisation, unlike morning practice (Learn Mem 2021). AOMI training at 8–10 pm ('early sleep') vs ≥12 h before sleep improved gait/balance in adults ~70 y (Sci Rep 2024; NCT05393700). This contradicts the gap's framing that the c0099 null is the main older-adult evidence. Still open: the specific within-evening manipulation (training ~1 h vs ~4 h before habitual bedtime, both tested at 24 h) in adults aged 60+, controlling time-of-testing.

The claim that the evidence 'relies on reviews and a single small nap trial' is wrong. Siengsukon & Boyd ran overnight sleep-vs-wake (evening/morning) experiments in chronic stroke vs age-matched controls on a continuous tracking task and found sleep-dependent offline gains after stroke (Neurorehabil Neural Repair 2009). A PSG study in 20 chronic stroke patients and 10 controls related sleep parameters to offline motor learning (Front Neurol 2015). In rats, recovery of SO-coupled spindles (and loss of isolated delta waves) tracked motor recovery after stroke (Cell Rep 2022). A human pilot measured disturbed laterality of SO–spindle nesting after stroke (Front Neurol 2023). The SMiLES longitudinal study (BMJ Open 2024; NCT05746260) is underway on sleep-dependent motor-sequence consolidation after stroke. NCT05843656 (completed, n=62) applied spindle-/SO-like stimulation during sleep in stroke patients and healthy older adults with spindle-density outcomes. Still open: whether perilesional SO–spindle coupling predicts overnight paretic-hand sequence gains in chronic stroke vs healthy older controls in a circadian-matched sleep/wake design.

Encoding strength has already been crossed experimentally with sleep vs wake in older adults. A 2025 UMass dissertation ('Sleep Benefits Procedural Motor Learning in Older Adults With Additional Practice') assigned young (18–24) and older (62–75) adults to standard training vs overtraining on an explicit SRTT before a 12-h interval of sleep or wake. As its title says, it reports that sleep benefits procedural learning in older adults when they get additional practice. Earlier SLEEP abstracts from the same programme (2020, 2024) report the overtraining × sleep design. Already answered: whether more training restores sleep-dependent SRTT gains in older adults. Still open: training to a fixed performance criterion (rather than a fixed number of extra blocks), circadian-controlled (counterbalanced AM/PM) designs, and adequate power.

The gap says a circadian-controlled design showed sleep improved accuracy but not speed 'in early PD and healthy older adults'. That is a misreading of c0050–c0052. In that paper only Experiment 1 (young adults) used the circadian-controlled MEM/EME sleep-vs-wake design. Experiment 2 (26 PD and 24 healthy older controls) was an overnight pre/post design with no wake comparison, so it cannot show a sleep-specific accuracy benefit in older adults. The motivating premise therefore rests on young-adult data only. Older-adult sleep/wake studies have also reported accuracy measures (e.g., Spencer et al. 2007; Wilson et al. 2012), which bears on the claim that the nulls rest on speed alone. The proposed reanalysis by accuracy remains open but is less strongly motivated.

The between-study version of the question is partly answered. A Bayesian meta-analysis (eLife 2024/25; 23 studies, 297 effect sizes) tested coupling phase, strength, percentage and spindle amplitude as predictors of consolidation. It identified age and memory type as moderators, and found that precise, strong frontal SO–fast-spindle coupling predicts consolidation. Coupling precision vs spindle power has been compared in younger vs older adults (Sci Rep 2019, associative memory). Coupling predicts gross-motor (juggling) learning across age groups (eLife 2022). So 'does the coupling–consolidation link differ by age and task type' has meta-analytic and cross-study evidence. Still open: a within-sample test in adults aged 60+ that pits coupling against fast-spindle density as competing predictors across a motor-sequence task and a cognitive procedural task (Tower of Hanoi).
